newsitem.title: USA: Cleveland says may drop Grigsby from future deals.
newsitem.headline: Cleveland says may drop Grigsby from future deals.

text.p: Cleveland's finance director said Tuesday she was rethinking the use of Grigsby Brandford & Co Inc on future bond issues, after the underwriter last month dropped out of a deal and prompted a costly delay.

The one-week delay in repricing the issue and rearranging the bond syndicate cost the city about $500,000 in savings that would have resulted from the original pricing, according to Finance Director Kathryn Burrer Hyer.
"I would be reluctant to have them in a lead role," Hyer said in an interview with Reuters.

Grigsby priced and then repriced the $82 million parking facilities refunding revenue bond issue on Aug 22, but the minority-owned firm then failed to extend a written offer for the bond purchase agreement, forcing the city to scrap the pricing, Hyer said.

She said the initial pricing resulted in some oversubscribed maturities, so Grigsby repriced the bonds at higher prices, resulting in the normal loss of some orders. The firm subsequently chose to bail out of the deal, which was insured by MBIA Inc's MBIA Insurance Corp.
"We were unable to reach an agreement and sign the bond purchase agreement," Hyer said.

She said she could only speculate as to why Grigsby refused to sign the agreement, saying that only Grigsby officials could answer that question. She added that she did not know how many unsold bonds Grigsby might have had in inventory after the repricing.
Executives with Grigsby have not returned repeated phone calls over the past week.
The deal was finally completed on Aug 29 with Travelers Group Inc's Smith Barney Inc in the senior manager slot and Grigsby reduced to a co-manager position.
Market participants said it is extremely rare for an underwriter to walk away from a deal because of the ill-will such a move creates with bond issuers.

Executives at some large underwriting firms have also questioned the capitalization levels of minority-owned firms like Grigsby, arguing that such firms are sometimes too thinly capitalized to weather market downturns and protect their clients from losses.
Hyer said that Grigsby's involvement on upcoming bond issues would be dependent on future circumstances and would be decided on "a case-by-case basis."
She added that Grigsby's role as a co-manager in an upcoming $15 million bond anticipation note deal to fund demolition costs of Cleveland's current football stadium was being reevaluated.
Delaying the parking bond issue exposed it to worsening market conditions last week, which ate into higher savings the city stood to gain from the Aug 22 pricing.
Hyer estimated the Aug 29 pricing of the bonds shaved $500,000 off the present value savings, which stood at $7.5 million when the deal was finally completed.
Still, Hyer said the city was happy with the level of savings finally achieved on the deal, calling it "phenominal."
"So people are happy about it despite going off step a bit," she said.
Market rumors of disclosure and other technical problems with the bond issue were apparently untrue. Hyer said that the documents for the Aug 22 pricing were the same as for the Aug 29 pricing.

Grigsby was chosen as senior manager for the issue after a request for proposals process, according to Hyer, who added that she believed it was the first time the San Francisco-based firm was tapped for the top slot in a city deal.
--Karen Pierog, 312-408-8647
